grammar.q: By the time the meeting started, Maya _____ the report.
grammar.why: Use the past perfect for an action completed before another past event.

grammar.q: If I _____ more time, I would take an advanced writing course.
grammar.why: The second conditional uses if + past simple, followed by would + base verb.

grammar.q: The final design _____ by the client tomorrow.
grammar.why: The future passive is will be + past participle.

grammar.q: The tutor recommended _____ the paragraph aloud.
grammar.why: Recommend is commonly followed by a gerund when no object is used.

grammar.q: I wish I _____ more carefully before sending that email.
grammar.why: Wish + past perfect expresses regret about a past action.

grammar.q: The team has worked on this project _____ March.
grammar.why: Use since with the starting point of a period.

grammar.q: The new website _____ at the moment.
grammar.why: Present continuous passive: am/is/are being + past participle.

grammar.q: Despite _____ several problems, the team met the deadline.
grammar.why: Despite is followed by a noun or gerund, not a finite clause.

grammar.q: She asked me where I _____ the reference image.
grammar.why: Reported questions use statement word order; the past perfect can show an earlier action.

grammar.q: If they had tested the prototype, they _____ the problem earlier.
grammar.why: The third conditional uses if + past perfect and would have + past participle.

reading.title: Designing with evidence
reading.text: A successful project rarely depends on one clever idea. It develops through observation, testing and decisions that respond to real needs. For this reason, teams should examine the context before choosing a solution. A method that works for one audience may create difficulties for another. Small tests can reveal problems that are difficult to notice from inside the project. They also give people a chance to explain what they actually need. It is important to distinguish between an assumption and evidence. An assumption may be a useful starting point, but it should not replace observation. The strongest approach is therefore flexible: it keeps a clear purpose while remaining open to new evidence.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A thoughtful process matters more than a single quick idea.
The most complex solution is always the best.
Research should happen only after a project is finished.
questions.why: The passage focuses on context, evidence, testing and thoughtful decisions.

choices: They remove the need for research.
They can reveal problems and real user needs.
They guarantee that the first idea will succeed.
questions.why: Testing reveals issues that may be hard to notice otherwise.

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about assumptions?
choices: They can be a starting point, but should be checked against evidence.
questions.why: The passage distinguishes assumptions from evidence.

questions.q: Which statement best matches the conclusion?
choices: Progress depends on using information meaningfully.
Progress means collecting as much material as possible.
Appearance is the only measure of quality.
questions.why: The conclusion emphasises evidence and a flexible, purposeful process.
